title: serving-runtime-architecture-kernel-scheduling-profiling-and-runbooks-2026-05-15
author: Aisha Malik
content:
Overview

This consolidated reference documents the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling rules, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes (selected), known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and platform leads responsible for deploying and operating Redwood's inference runtime.

Key goals:
- Provide a single authoritative reference for architecture and operational procedures.
- Give reproducible profiling and benchmarking steps to validate performance changes.
- Capture kernel-scheduling and batching heuristics to maintain predictable latency and throughput.
- Include runbooks for common incidents and postmortem links.

Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary:
- The runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine composed of: request router, front-end workers, scheduler, kernel execution pool, KV cache service, and telemetry/observer.
- Design priorities: low tail latency (p50/p95/p99), predictable throughput, graceful degradation, and cost efficiency via batching/caching/quantization.

Components:
1) Request Router (redwood-router):
   - Responsibilities: auth, routing policy (region/tier/model-variant), early rejection, and metrics tagging.
   - SLOs: 50ms median, 200ms p99 for routing decisions.

2) Front-end Workers (fe-worker):
   - Tasks: tokenize, prompt preprocessing, policy checks (safety, truncation), and routing to scheduler.
   - Concurrency: typically 256 concurrent lightweight goroutines per instance.

3) Scheduler (schedd):
   - Responsibilities: build execution batches, KV cache lookup/insert, GPU assignment, and fallback to cheaper model variants.
   - Heuristics: dynamic batch sizing based on recent latency window and model profile. See Kernel scheduling section.

4) Kernel Execution Pool (kernpool):
   - Runs compiled kernels (fused attention, matmul kernels) optimized per model/quantization.
   - Supports synchronous and asynchronous execution paths.

5) KV Cache Service (kv-cache):
   - Provides per-session prefix caching with TTL and memory quotas. Used for streaming and chat workloads.

6) Telemetry & Observer (telemon):
   - Emits token-level latency, per-request CPU/GPU utilization, memory high-watermarks, and tail allocation traces to observability backend.

Cross-cutting guarantees:
- Model variants are annotated with performance profile tags (seq_len, kv_ratio, compute_cost). Routing uses these to select compatible fallback models.
- Autoscaling is driven primarily by SLO breach signals (p95 latency > target) and queued request depth.

Kernel scheduling (rules and heuristics)

Objective: maximize GPU utilization and throughput while preserving latency SLOs for customer-facing tiers.

Core rules:
- Latency-first ordering for latency-tier requests: priority queue with max-batch = min(32, target_batch_by_model).
- Throughput ordering for batch-tier jobs: batch up to model-specific max_batch (often 128-512) and use background slots.
- Mixed workloads: use dual-queue scheduler. Latency queue preempts throughput queue if predicted p95 would exceed target.

Heuristics used by schedd:
- Adaptive batch sizing: compute target_batch = clamp(base_batch * sqrt(1 + recent_qps / base_qps), 1, max_batch).
- Sequence-length bucketing: group requests with similar seq_len (±16 tokens) to reduce padding waste.
- KV-cache affinity: requests with cache hits are favored for smaller batches to avoid unnecessary padding.
- Kernel selection: prefer quantized kernels when (expected latency delta < 8ms and quality delta within monitored regression thresholds).

Configuration table (defaults)
| config_key | default | description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| base_batch_for_model:<model> | 16 | baseline batch for model architecture |
| max_batch_for_model:<model> | 256 | maximum allowed batch |
| latency_preempt_threshold_ms | 10 | if adding a request would add this much to p95 prediction, preempt throughput queue |
| seq_len_bucket_size | 16 | token window for bucketing |

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run: before merging performance-impacting changes (kernels, batching logic, memory allocs) or when investigating unexplained SLO regressions.

Prerequisites:
- Access to perf cluster (perf-ops project).
- Dataset and load profiles stored under s3://redwood-perfbench/<model>/<profile>.
- Local copy of the benchmarking harness (git repo: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-bench).

Procedure (minimally reproducible):
1) Snapshot current canary image and baseline metrics:
   - Record p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU util, and allocation traces for 30m.
   - Command: benchctl snapshot --cluster perf --model <model> --profile <profile> --out baseline.json
2) Deploy candidate image to an isolated perf pool with same hardware SKU.
   - Use staged rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 100% to validate at scale.
3) Run identical load profile for 60 minutes. Capture traces.
   - Command: benchctl run --target perf-pool --model <model> --profile <profile> --duration 60m --out candidate.json
4) Automated diff and triage:
   - benchctl compare baseline.json candidate.json --metrics latency,p99,tokens_per_sec,gpu_util --thresholds "p95:+3%,p99:+5%"
   - If regression flagged, capture heap/alloc traces and escalate to kernel team.
5) Kernel-level profiling (if regression):
   - Use nvprof/nsys on a representative worker: nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt --output kernel-profile.qdrep -- ./kernpool --model <model>
   - Capture per-kernel times and memory copies.
6) Action items: revert, tune batch heuristics, or adjust kernel launch parameters. Document findings in a benchmarking PR.

Benchmarking suite (overview)

Artifacts and locations:
- Benchmark harness: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-bench (contains load generators, profiles, and comparison tools).
- Dataset catalog: s3://redwood-perfbench/catalog.json (describes profiles: short-streaming, chat-burst, long-completion).
- Standard hardware SKUs: p4d.24xlarge (H100), a100-80gb, trn-1 (internal TPU-like).

Standard profiles:
- chat-burst: many short requests (avg 40 tokens), bursty qps pattern.
- long-completion: fewer requests, long seq_len (avg 2048 tokens).
- embedding-bulk: large batched embedding jobs.

Success criteria for a benchmark run:
- No SLO regression beyond thresholds defined in the bench config.
- Token/sec >= baseline * (1 - allowed_delta).
- GPU utilization within expected curve (not >95% sustained for >10 minutes unless intentional).

Release notes (selected items, v2026.05)

v2026.05 (2026-05-10) - highlights:
- Improved adaptive batching algorithm to reduce p99 for chat-burst by ~12% in perf cluster.
- New fused attention kernel (attention-fused-v2) deployed behind feature flag. ~8% throughput improvement on H100.
- KV-cache eviction bug fixed where long-lived sessions caused unbounded memory growth. Root cause: TTL not applied on session handoff.
- Added benchctl compare thresholds and automatic regression labeling in CI.

Notes for operators:
- attention-fused-v2 is behind flag: set X_REDWOOD_KERNEL=attention-fused-v2 to enable on node pools for testing.
- If enabling widely, run a night-run benchmark on a representative 100-node pool and validate p99/p95.

Known issues (current)

1) Intermittent p99 spikes under cross-tenant noisy neighbor workloads (INC-2026-112):
   - Symptom: p99 latency spikes by 2-4x for latency-tier requests when throughput-tier background load surges.
   - Mitigation: enable stricter latency preemption (set latency_preempt_threshold_ms=5). Longer-term: reserve hardware isolation for tier-1 customers.

2) Memory leak in fe-worker v1.42.2 (fixed in v1.42.4):
   - Symptom: fe-worker RSS grows slowly over ~48-72 hours under heavy chat workloads.
   - Workaround: restart fe-worker every 24 hours on older fleets.

3) Quantized kernel numerical drift for edge-case tokenization patterns (QA-2026-89):
   - Symptom: rare decoding divergence on very long sequences when using 4-bit kernels.
   - Mitigation: fall back to float16 kernel for requests > 4096 tokens or for customer cohorts flagged for strict determinism.

Runbooks (operational procedures)

A) High p99 latency for latency-tier (incident triage)
1) Scope
   - Identify affected model(s), region(s), and customer tiers.
2) Quick checks (first 10 mins):
   - Check metrics: schedd queue depth, p50/p95/p99, GPU util across pool.
   - Command: telemon query "SELECT * FROM request_metrics WHERE service='schedd' AND pool='<pool>' LAST 15m"
3) Immediate mitigations (order matters):
   - Increase preemption aggressiveness: set latency_preempt_threshold_ms to 5 and restart schedd.
   - Drain throughput queue slots: scale down batch workers or throttle batch-tier routes.
   - If problem persists: failover to fallback model variant (lower-cost but compatible).
4) Post-incident steps:
   - Capture traces, annotate the incident, and run full profiling playbook.

B) GPU OOM on kernpool node
1) Symptoms: oom errors in kernpool logs, node enters NotReady.
2) Triage:
   - Check last model deployed and kernel flags.
   - Run: kubectl logs node/kernpool-<id> --since=1h | grep -i oom
3) Mitigations:
   - Temporarily cordon node and remove from pool: kubectl cordon node/kernpool-<id>
   - Rebalance sessions: trigger session handoff.
   - If recurrent: lower max_batch_for_model for that node's pool and escalate to kernel team.

C) KV-cache memory pressure
1) Detection: high memory pressure alerts for kv-cache (mem > 80%).
2) Mitigation:
   - Reduce per-session cache size: set KV_CACHE_MAX_PER_SESSION to 4MB.
   - Aggressively expire old sessions: set default TTL to 12h for non-enterprise pools.

Team wiki and ownership

- Primary owners: serving-runtime (team) -> rotation owners: runtime-oncall@redwood.internal
- Kernel team: kernel-dev@redwood.internal (owns kernel tuning and fused-kernel PRs).
- Performance team: perf-eng@redwood.internal (owns bench profiles and perf cluster).

Useful links:
- Bench harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-bench
- Perf S3 catalog: s3://redwood-perfbench/catalog.json
- Incident tracker: internal JIRA board RED-RUNTIME

Maintenance & roadmap notes
- Upcoming (Q3 2026): multi-tenant isolation lanes (hardware reservations) and deterministic quantization path to reduce numerical drift.
- Ongoing: expand bench profiles to cover multi-modal workloads (image+text).

Appendix: cheatsheet commands
- benchctl snapshot --cluster perf --model <model> --profile <profile> --out baseline.json
- benchctl run --target perf-pool --model <model> --profile <profile> --duration 60m --out candidate.json
- benchctl compare baseline.json candidate.json --metrics latency,p99,tokens_per_sec,gpu_util --thresholds "p95:+3%,p99:+5%"
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt --output kernel-profile.qdrep -- ./kernpool --model <model>

If you find gaps or contradictions, open a documentation PR and tag owners listed above.
